name: Humane
epitaph: Meant to replace your phone. Ended up in a drawer.
oneLiner: Ex-Apple founders built the AI Pin, a screenless clip-on gadget you talked to, which projected text onto your palm.
causeOfDeath: The $699 AI Pin drew harsh reviews and overheating complaints; buyers returned it, sales hit a tenth of plan, and HP bought the team for $116M.
moneyNote: Over $230M raised (TechCrunch, 2023); TechCrunch later put it at $240M. No valuation was confirmed; in 2024 it reportedly sought a $750M–$1B sale. HP paid $116M in 2025.
inOneMinute: Two star ex-Apple employees raised **over $230 million** to build the AI Pin, a $699 clip-on AI assistant meant to free you from your phone.
Reviews were brutal. It sold **about 10,000 units against a goal of 100,000**, and for a while returns outpaced sales.
In February 2025 HP bought the team and patents for **$116 million**, and every AI Pin was switched off ten days later.
killerLine: To replace something people already love, **you must be better at the everyday basics**, not just more futuristic.

chapters.title: The idea: life after the smartphone
chapters.body: Imran Chaudhri spent about 20 years as a designer at Apple. Bethany Bongiorno was a director of software engineering for iOS and macOS. In 2018 they left that world to start Humane, with a big belief: **phones keep our heads down and our attention trapped**. They wanted a device that could disappear. Their answer was the AI Pin, a small square that clipped magnetically to your shirt. It had **no screen**. You spoke to it, and an AI answered. A tiny laser projected text, like who was calling, onto your palm. It had a camera and its own mobile connection, so it could work without a smartphone. About 90 ex-Apple staff worked there at some point.

chapters.title: The rise: hype before the product
chapters.body: Humane came out of stealth in September 2021 with a $100 million round, then raised **another $100 million in March 2023**, bringing the total to $230 million. Backers included Microsoft, Qualcomm, LG, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and OpenAI's technology would power the AI. Humane built buzz like a fashion brand: the Pin debuted on a Paris Fashion Week runway in September 2023. TIME even listed it among the best inventions of 2023, before anyone outside had reviewed it. In November 2023 it launched at **$699 plus $24 a month** for the AI service and a mobile connection on T-Mobile's network. Shipping slipped to April 2024.

chapters.title: The cracks: reviews, returns and a fire risk
chapters.body: When reviewers got the Pin in April 2024, the verdicts were largely negative. A New York Times investigation later described problems including overheating. After the reviews, **over 1,000 pre-orders were cancelled**. By August 2024 Humane had sold about 10,000 Pins against a hope of 100,000 in year one, and about 3,000 had been returned. Internal documents showed that for a while **returns outpaced new sales**. In June 2024 Humane told customers to stop using its charging case, as some batteries from one supplier might be **a fire hazard**. Meanwhile it was reportedly trying to sell itself for $750 million to $1 billion.

chapters.title: The fall: switched off from the cloud
chapters.body: In October 2024 Humane cut the price to $499. It also demoed its AI software for cars, phones and speakers, hoping to become a software company. It wasn't enough. On 18 February 2025, HP agreed to buy Humane's engineers, its CosmOS software and over 300 patents for **$116 million, less than half of the money Humane had raised**. HP did not want the Pin. Because the Pin depended on Humane's servers, **every device stopped working on 28 February 2025**: no calls, no messages, no AI. Only buyers from the last 90 days got refunds. The founders joined a new HP lab called HP IQ. Some staff got big raises; others lost their jobs that night.

charts.title: AI Pin: plan vs reality
charts.takeaway: Humane reached about a tenth of its goal, and nearly a third of buyers sent their Pin back.

mistakes.title: Launched before the product was ready
mistakes.explain: Reviews of the Pin were largely negative, and reports described problems including overheating. **First impressions became the story**: over 1,000 pre-orders were cancelled, and about 3,000 of 10,000 buyers returned it. With hardware you get one launch, and a product that isn't ready, sold at $699, burns the brand.

mistakes.title: Tried to replace the phone instead of adding to it
mistakes.explain: The Pin had its own mobile connection and a $24 monthly plan, asking people to carry and pay for a second device. Yet the phone in their pocket already did calls, messages, photos and AI answers. **A new device needs one job it does far better than what people already own**, and buyers didn't find it.

mistakes.title: Hype ran far ahead of proof
mistakes.explain: A fashion-week runway debut and a TIME 'best inventions' listing came before any independent reviews. **Big expectations made the fall harder.** Humane reportedly hoped to sell itself for up to $1 billion; it ended at $116 million, less than half of what investors had put in.

mistakes.title: A device that died with its servers
mistakes.explain: The Pin needed Humane's cloud for almost everything. When HP bought the team but not the device, **every Pin stopped working within ten days**, and only recent buyers got refunds. Cloud-dependent hardware puts customers at risk if the company fails.

warningSigns: Are you asking customers to give up something they love (like their phone) for a product that does less?
Are you about to launch even though testers still complain about speed or reliability?
Is your launch buzz coming from events and awards rather than from real users?
Are returns or cancellations rising faster than new orders?
Will your product stop working completely if your servers go down?

lessons.title: Beat the incumbent at one daily task
lessons.detail: Pick one thing people do every day and make it clearly faster or easier than the phone. Win that before promising a whole new way of life.

lessons.title: Let a few strangers test before you ship
lessons.detail: Give 50 outsiders your product for two weeks and ask brutally honest questions. Their complaints are tomorrow's reviews.

lessons.title: Keep hype in step with reality
lessons.detail: Runways and awards are great, but only after the product is solid. Under-promise publicly, then surprise people.

lessons.title: Track returns as closely as sales
lessons.detail: A rising return rate is the loudest signal that something is wrong. Look at it every week, and talk to every customer who sends one back.

lessons.title: Plan an offline or exit mode
lessons.detail: If your gadget relies on your servers, decide how customers keep using it if you shut down. It protects them and your reputation.

afterlife.text: HP folded Humane's engineers, its CosmOS software and over 300 patents into a new lab, HP IQ, with founders Imran Chaudhri and Bethany Bongiorno joining it. Some software engineers got raises of 30% to 70%, while staff closest to the Pin were laid off. AI Pins stopped working on 28 February 2025 and owners were told to recycle them.
